It is a matter of profound spiritual gravity to sit with the “unsearchable riches” of Christ while witnessing the “noise and tumult” of a world that defines human worth by a “string of degrees,” a “pulpit-throne,” or a “balanced checkbook,” and I must ask you with a gentle spirit: why do you ask after the nature of work and dignity in this hour? [13, 317, 434, 1503, 1605, Conversation History]. Are you perhaps feeling “overwhelmed and desperate” by the “drudgery” of a labor that feels like a “horrible pit,” or are you seeking a “settled certainty” to anchor your soul in the truth that you are a “vessel for honor” whose daily breath is a “lavish endowment” from the King? [11, 14, 20, 54, 1143, 1450, 1605, Conversation History]. In a day when many “shave off the edges” of the truth to offer “spiritual placebos” like the “prosperity gospel,” we must return to the “external Word” to see how the Lord personally governs the “vicissitudes of life” by reminding us that we were “bought at a price” [1, 11, 28, 437, 1138, 1503, 1515, Conversation History].

The Reformed tradition teaches that “God personally and exhaustively pervades and sustains and governs every aspect of His creation,” and therefore, your capacity to labor is not an “administrative anomaly” but a reflection of the “image of the One who created him” (Colossians 3:10) [15, 34, 68, 1143, 1532, 1720, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 1: The Blueprint of Dignity (The Image of God)**

**Verse**
“Then God said, ‘Let Us make man in Our image, according to Our likeness; let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the air, and over the cattle, over all the earth and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.’ So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them” (Genesis 1:26–27). [1006, 1068, 1286, 1313, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The sources teach that humanity is the “crowning point of creation,” and the *Imago Dei* defines our “unique relation to God,” setting us “apart from the animals” [1068, 1313, 1322, Conversation History]. This image means we possess “reason... intellect, will, and emotion,” allowing us to be “living being[s] capable of embodying God’s communicable attributes” [472, 1068, 1322, Conversation History]. Because “the masterpiece of creation, a human being, was made in God’s image,” our dignity is not earned by “achievement, insights, and wisdom” but is inherent from the moment the Lord “breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living being” (Genesis 2:7) [434, 474, 684, 1010, 1328, 1406, 1531, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You should “not be deceived” by “worldly philosophies” that measure your worth by “numerical growth” or “property,” for “your life is not your own” because you were “bought at a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20) [12, 91, 101, 1138, 1233, 1262, 1406, 1502, 1670, Conversation History]. Recognize that you are a “new creation” in Christ, and your dignity rests in being a “fellow citizen with the saints and member of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19) [287, 290, 783, 903, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Jewish vs. Gentile Context**
In the ancient **theocratic context**, “national greatness” and “large and beautiful cities” were “temporal signs” of God’s favor, yet the Jews were reminded that “man shall not live by bread alone; but man lives by every word that proceeds from the mouth of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 8:3) [409, 574, 914, 986, 1313, 1353, 1519, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our standing, showing that we are “sojourners and pilgrims” whose “citizenship is in heaven” and whose goal is to be “conformed to the image of His Son” (Philippians 3:20; Romans 8:29) [13, 26, 38, 142, 440, 893, 1203, 1313, 1320, 1426, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 2: Work as Pre-Fall Worship**

**Verse**
“Then the LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to tend and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). [1011, 1077, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The Reformed tradition asserts that “work was an important and dignified part of representing the image of God and serving Him, even before the Fall” [1077, Conversation History]. Labor is not an “administrative anomaly” brought on by sin, but a “spiritual service of worship” meant to bring “glory to His name” [11, 15, 992, 1101, Conversation History]. Before the curse, work was without “drudgery,” for “God saw everything that He had made, and indeed it was very good” (Genesis 1:31) [54, 1008, 1071, Conversation History]. To “tend and keep” was an act of “stewardship,” as all our “aptitudes and faculties are given to us... for His glory” [120, 121, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You must “discipline your mind” to see that “whatever you do, do all to the glory of God,” whether you are “cooking food” or “harvesting grain” (1 Corinthians 10:31) [116, 132, 195, 1406, 1709, Conversation History]. “Trade in your worry for trust,” knowing that work is a “lavish endowment” by which we “adorn the doctrine of God” in the “mundane area” of life (Titus 2:10) [11, 33, 36, 94, 201, 1072, 1131, 1143, 1408, 1515, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Ritual vs. Reality**
Under the **Mosaic Law**, the “Sabbath” was a “sacred ordained day” to model God’s rest, yet the Pharisees turned it into a “minefield” of “unwritten... taboos” [59, 1072, 1253, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** this, revealing that “everything the Sabbath signified has been completely fulfilled in the finished work of Christ,” granting us a “repose of the soul” that allows us to work from a position of rest rather than for a “form of gleaning” (Hebrews 4:10) [13, 17, 24, 59, 61, 62, 136, 142, 1253, 1445, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 3: The Distortion of the Curse (Work as Toil)**

**Verse**
“Then to Adam He said, ‘Because you have heeded the voice of your wife, and have eaten from the tree of which I commanded you, saying, “You shall not eat of it”: Cursed is the ground for your sake; In toil you shall eat of it All the days of your life. Both thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you, And you shall eat the herb of the field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread Till you return to the ground, For out of it you were taken; For dust you are, And to dust you shall return’ ” (Genesis 3:17–19). [1017, 1090, 1562, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The “record of history” shows that sin “rendered laborious” what was intended to be a delight, turning work into an “arduous grind” where “there is no end to all his labors” (Ecclesiastes 4:8) [54, 58, 670, 857, 1209, 1338, Conversation History]. The Reformed tradition notes that the curse did not invent work, but made it “reluctant,” as “the carnal mind is enmity against God” [1090, 1333, 1500, Conversation History]. When we “love the gifts more than the Giver,” we fall into “sinful self-indulgence,” seeking “individual accomplishment” as a “platform for your own ego” rather than “ascribing greatness to our God” (Deuteronomy 32:3; 1 John 2:15) [12, 51, 64, 108, 130, 133, 168, 765, 873, 1058, 1406, 1623, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You should “not look for some other fountain of knowledge” in “career” success to satisfy your soul, for “one’s life does not consist in the abundance of the things he possesses” (Luke 12:15) [51, 123, 298, 1222, 1341, 1406, 1503, Conversation History]. Recognize that “godliness with contentment is great gain,” and you must “hold fast and not let go” of the truth that “your labor is not in vain in the Lord” (1 Timothy 6:6; 1 Corinthians 15:58) [10, 116, 143, 461, 954, 1153, 1406, 1709, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Continuity of the Decree**
In the ancient **Jewish context**, “testifying in a dispute” required “two or three witnesses” to establish “justice for all,” protecting the laborer from being “rob[bed] . . . by fraud” (Exodus 23:1; James 5:4) [330, 367, 691, 937, 1072, 1174, 1189, 1213, 1317, 1365, 1473, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our "wages," teaching that while “the laborer is worthy of his hire,” our true “inheritance [is] incorruptible,” and we must “refuse to yield submission” to any master who “shares in . . . evil deeds” (1 Peter 1:4; 2 John 11) [13, 21, 26, 78, 1188, 1313, 1426, 1466, 1515, 1529, 1646, 1720, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 4: The Meaning of Labor in the New Creation**

**Verse**
“And there shall be no more curse, but the throne of God and of the Lamb shall be in it, and His servants shall serve Him” (Revelation 22:3). [190, 200, 276, 294, 997, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
Scripture handles the “noise and tumult” of earthly careers by pointing to the “consummation of history,” where “Christ ultimately crushes the kingdoms of men and establishes His own” [13, 20, 21, 103, 1199, 1315, 1515, 1720, Conversation History]. In the “new heaven and new earth,” labor is restored to its “spotless purity,” for “heaven is not a place of eternal boredom and tedious inactivity; it is filled with... expanded opportunities for service” [117, 419, 421, 997, Conversation History]. Believers, as “slaves of God,” will “joyfully worship and exalt our heavenly Master” through eternal “spiritual effort and spiritual enterprise” [190, 200, 293, 302, 591, Conversation History]. This reveals that “nothing thwarts any aspect of His plan,” as even our “momentary, light affliction” in work is “producing for us an eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:17) [5, 11, 21, 286, 718, 1132, 1408, 1515, 1572, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
“Wait for His Son from heaven,” knowing that “perfect justice will come” and the “Lord knows those who are His” (1 Thessalonians 1:10; 2 Timothy 2:19) [11, 14, 24, 101, 147, 176, 201, 211, 352, 412, 1132, 1138, 1143, 1315, 1408, 1450, 1515, 1720, Conversation History]. You should find “tranquility of soul” by “resting upon the surest foundation,” for if you are “faithful in what is least,” you will be “honored for [your] faithfulness” when you “enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25:21; Luke 16:10) [11, 24, 116, 129, 206, 209, 279, 282, 286, 299, 412, 1132, 1143, 1408, 1450, 1515, 1720, Conversation History].

***

**Final Reminder**
“Nevertheless the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal, ‘The Lord knows those who are His,’ and, ‘Everyone who names the name of the Lord is to abstain from wickedness’ ” (2 Timothy 2:19). [11, 147, 176, 201, 211, 222, 285, 300, 313, 324, 332, 335, 361, 405, 413, 414, 424, 444, 449, 591, 1138, 1407, 1441, 1450, Conversation History].

references.cited_text: One passage that refers to both the spiritual and physical aspects of our lives is 2 Corinthians 9. The context of this passage refers to believers’ generosity concerning the needs of the saints: We are to give “not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (v. 7). As we reveal our own desire to provide for the needs of others (v. 6), God “who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness” (v. 10). When you invest in God’s kingdom, He will provide not only spiritual fruit but also bread for food.

Further observing that Jesus’ own telling of the prodigal son parable ends without resolution, the article suggests that this “reveals the open-endedness of the Kingdom of God.” What’s more, the story’s true ending “is the end of my story, your story, and everyone’s story—beyond our wildest dreams.” By such a wholly subjective approach, Jesus’ stories become playthings to be bent and shaped into whatever form suits the hearer’s fancy. Jesus’ whole message becomes versatile, subjective, and infinitely adaptable to the felt needs and personal preferences of each hearer.

Complete Submission Being a slave not only meant belonging to someone else; it also meant being always available to obey that person in every way. The slave’s sole duty was to carry out the master’s wishes, and the faithful slave was eager to do so without hesitation or complaint. After all, “slaves know no law but their master’s word; they have no rights of their own; they are absolute possessions of their master; and they are bound to give their master unquestioning obedience.”15 Building on this imagery, the New Testament repeatedly calls believers to faithfully obey the Master. Hence, Paul could ask the Roman believers, “Who are you to judge the servant of another? To his own master he stands or falls; and he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand” (Rom. 14:4). He could tell the Philippians that “to live is Christ” (Phil. 1:21) and that “whatever things were gain to me, those things I have counted as loss for the sake of Christ” (Phil. 3:7). To the Galatians, Paul could exclaim, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20); and to the Corinthians he could declare that those transformed by the gospel “no longer live for themselves, but for Him who died and rose again on their behalf ” (2 Cor. 5:15). Elsewhere, he exhorted his readers with these words: “Do you not know . . . that you are not your own? For you have been bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:19–20).

The apostle Paul used that same imagery when speaking directly to physical slaves and their human owners. In Ephesians 6:5–9, he wrote: Slaves, be obedient to those who are your masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, in the sincerity of your heart, as to Christ; not by way of eyeservice, as men-pleasers, but as slaves of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart. With good will render service, as to the Lord, and not to men, knowing that whatever good thing each one does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether slave or free. And masters, do the same things to them, and give up threatening, knowing that both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no partiality with Him.

Our study of slavery has reminded us that we were once the wretched slaves of the cruelest master imaginable—sin. As members of a fallen human race, we were bound, blind, and dead in our disobedience and rebellion. It was in the midst of our helplessness and hopelessness that God intervened. Being rich in mercy, He chose us, set His love on us, and rescued us from the clutches of our former owner. Through Christ’s sacrificial death, we were redeemed from the slave market of sin. God cleansed us from our iniquity, clothed us in His righteousness, and welcomed us into His household forever.

All of this underscores the magnanimous character of our loving Master. His bondage is true freedom. His yoke is easy and His burden is light. What He has required, He has also enabled by His grace. And He calls us to obey, not because He needs us but because He knows that we need Him. After all, it is only in relationship with Him that our souls can be satisfied. Only by delighting in Him can we experience true joy and eternal life. As Augustine famously prayed in his Confessions, “You awake us to delight in praising You, for You have made us for Yourself, and our hearts are restless until they find their rest in You.”12

Take a look at yourself; you are a creature, acknowledge the creator; you are a slave, do not disdain the master; you have been adopted, but not on your merits. Seek the glory of the one from whom you have received this grace, O adopted child, seek the glory of the one whose glory was sought by his only true born Son.12 Charles Hodge (1797–1878) All Christians . . . were bought with a price. That is, purchased by Christ with his most precious blood, 1 Pet. 1, 18.19. Ye belong to him; ye are his slaves, and should therefore act accordingly; and not be the slaves of men. The slave of one master cannot be the slave of another. One who is redeemed by Christ, who feels that he belongs to him, that his will is the supreme rule of action, and who performs all his duties, not as a man-pleaser, but as doing service as to the Lord, and not to men, Eph. 6, 6. 7, is inwardly free, whatever his external relations may be. . . . They [the Corinthian believers] all belonged to Christ. To him their allegiance was due. They, therefore, whether bond or free, should act in obedience to him, and not in obedience to men.13
